column1: How does ordinary inference differ from model training in terms of parameter modification?
column2: Training updates the model's numerical parameters based on prediction errors, whereas ordinary inference executes calculations using existing, fixed parameters without altering them. (Section 1.2)

column1: How does inserting a custom definition into a prompt context affect underlying model weights?
column2: It does not alter model weights; prompt definitions only provide temporary information available to the current inference calculation. (Section 1.2)

column1: What structural component changes during training or fine-tuning compared to sending a new prompt message?
column2: Training or fine-tuning changes the model's internal parameters, whereas a new prompt message changes only the context information available for that inference run. (Section 1.2)

column1: How does Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) supply updated information without retraining the model?
column2: RAG searches external document collections and appends retrieved passages into the input context, allowing a model with fixed parameters to answer based on new data. (Section 1.7)

column1: What is the primary difference between the pretraining process and standard inference execution?
column2: Pretraining uses optimization algorithms to adjust parameters and minimize prediction errors across training examples, while inference computes an output distribution for a given context using static parameters. (Section 1.2)

column1: Why does adding a document to a prompt context fail to prove that a model has learned permanent new knowledge?
column2: Providing a document in context only alters the active inference input; it does not update or retrain the model's underlying parameters. (Section 1.2)

column1: How does supplying a new factual claim via RAG differ from instilling that claim through fine-tuning?
column2: RAG supplies the factual claim as external text inside the context window of a fixed model, whereas fine-tuning modifies the model's internal parameters through training updates. (Section 1.2 & Section 1.7)

column1: Why does altering the context from a real-world task to a fictional scenario change the generated response without erasing model knowledge?
column2: Changing context modifies the input sequence and resulting conditional probabilities during inference, without altering the stored parameters of the model. (Section 1.7)

column1: What is the operational difference between parameter memory and external RAG retrieval?
column2: Parameter memory consists of internal learned numerical values stored in the model, whereas RAG dynamically fetches text passages from an external repository to include in the context window. (Section 1.2 & Section 1.7)

column1: Why are future isolated user sessions unaffected when a user provides new definitions during a single chat session?
column2: Chat messages only modify the temporary conversation context for current inference runs and do not trigger parameter updates in the underlying model. (Section 1.2)

column1: How does instruction tuning differ from standard prompt context modification?
column2: Instruction tuning updates the model's parameters using human demonstrations or preferences, whereas prompt modification only changes the input string supplied during inference. (Section 1.2)

column1: What methodology allows researchers to isolate the exact effect of context variations on output distributions?
column2: Keeping the model parameters fixed while systematically varying the input text and settings across inference runs. (Section 1.2)

column1: How does a document retrieval failure in a RAG pipeline differ from a model hallucination?
column2: A retrieval failure occurs when the external search mechanism selects irrelevant or missing text passages, whereas a hallucination occurs when model calculations generate unsupported or inaccurate output. (Section 1.7)

column1: What role do fixed parameters play during a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) step?
column2: The fixed parameters process the combined prompt context—including the original query and the retrieved external passages—to calculate output token probabilities. (Section 1.2 & Section 1.7)

column1: Why does citing an external reference in a generated text response not prove that the underlying model parameters were updated?
column2: Citations are often generated because external documents were retrieved and inserted into the active context window, not because the model's weight parameters were modified. (Section 1.7)

column1: What sequential path represents the flow of information in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) process?
column2: A user question triggers document retrieval, retrieved passages are combined with the question into a context prompt, and a fixed model uses that context to generate an answer. (Section 1.2 & Section 1.7)

column1: Why doesn't generating a fluent continuation update a model's stored weights?
column2: Continuation generation is strictly forward inference using existing parameters; parameter updates require an explicit optimization training step driven by prediction errors. (Section 1.2)

column1: What state do parameters hold prior to undergoing pretraining optimization?
column2: Parameters begin as initial numerical values that do not yet represent structured or readable encyclopedic knowledge until optimized against learning signals. (Section 1.2)
